stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
print("Plan the trip")

def book_hotel():
    print("Hotel booked")

def book_train():
    print("Train booked")
    book_hotel()

book_train()
print("Pack the bags")
output:
Plan the trip
Train booked
Hotel booked
Pack the bags

options.text:
Plan the trip
Hotel booked
Train booked
Pack the bags
options.rationale: This follows the order of the definitions. What counts is the order of the calls: `book_train()` prints before it calls `book_hotel()`.

options.text:
Plan the trip
Train booked
Pack the bags
options.rationale: The call `book_hotel()` inside `book_train` runs too, every time `book_train` is called.

options.text:
Plan the trip
Train booked
Hotel booked
Pack the bags
options.rationale: The `def` lines print nothing; `book_train()` prints, then calls `book_hotel()`, and then the last line runs.

options.text:
Plan the trip
Hotel booked
Train booked
Hotel booked
Pack the bags
options.rationale: A `def` only remembers the function; its body doesn't run when the definition is read.

explanation: Python runs the file from top to bottom. It prints `Plan the trip`, then reads the two `def` statements without running their bodies. The call `book_train()` prints `Train booked` and then calls `book_hotel()`, which prints `Hotel booked`. When the call finishes, Python continues after it and prints `Pack the bags`.

stem: A program prints the same three-line receipt header in five places. How does moving those lines into one function make the program easier to maintain?

options.text: A change to the header is made once, in the function, and every call gets it
options.rationale: The steps live in one place, so one fix updates all five places that call the function.

options.text: The header lines no longer need indentation, because the function groups them
options.rationale: A function body must be indented. Functions don't remove indentation rules.

options.text: The lines inside a function run faster than the same lines written outside it
options.rationale: Functions are about organising code, not speed. The same lines do the same work.

options.text: Each call can come before the `def`, so the order of the file doesn't matter any more
options.rationale: A function must be defined before a call to it runs, so order still matters.

explanation: Functions support decomposition (splitting a job into named steps), reuse (writing code once, calling it many times) and maintainability. With the header in one function, a change, such as a new shop name, is made in one place and every call uses it. Without the function, all five copies would need the same edit.

stem: Which function definition line is valid?

options.rationale: A function name, like any identifier, must not start with a digit.
`-` is the minus operator, so it can't be part of a name.
`def`, a valid snake_case name, empty brackets and the colon.
The brackets are needed even when the function takes nothing.

explanation: A definition line is `def`, then a name, then brackets, then a colon. Function names follow the same rules as variable names: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit, and not a keyword. Only `def second_course():` gets every part right.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
def water_garden():
    print("Fill the can")
    print("Water the roses")
print("Garden done")

water_garden()
output:
Garden done
Fill the can
Water the roses

options.text:
Fill the can
Water the roses
Garden done
options.rationale: `print("Garden done")` is not indented, so it is not in the body. It runs before the call.
The call `water_garden()` at the end does run the body.

options.text:
Garden done
Fill the can
Water the roses
Garden done
options.rationale: The unindented line runs only once, when Python reaches it; it is not part of the function.

options.text:
Garden done
Fill the can
Water the roses
options.rationale: The body is the two indented lines. The unindented `print` runs first, and the call runs the body afterwards.

explanation: The body of a function is the indented lines below the `def` line. The first line that is not indented, `print("Garden done")`, ends the function and runs straight away. Only after that does the call `water_garden()` run the two body lines.

stem: What happens when this code is run?
code:
print("Opening shop")
greet_customer()

def greet_customer():
    print("Welcome!")

options.text: `Opening shop` and `Welcome!` are printed, as Python reads the whole file first
options.rationale: Python reads the whole file for syntax, but it only creates the function when it runs the `def` line.

options.text: `Opening shop` is printed, and then a `NameError` stops the program
options.rationale: The call runs before the `def` line has run, so the name `greet_customer` doesn't exist yet.

options.text: Nothing is printed: Python reports a `SyntaxError` before running anything
options.rationale: The code follows Python's grammar, so it starts running. The problem only shows up at the call.

options.text: Only `Opening shop` is printed, and the early call is skipped without an error
options.rationale: Python never skips a call silently. An unknown name raises an error.

explanation: Python runs the file from top to bottom. It prints `Opening shop`, then reaches the call `greet_customer()`. The `def` line further down hasn't run yet, so the name is unknown and Python raises `NameError: name 'greet_customer' is not defined`. A function must be defined before the line that calls it runs.

stem: Which lines, placed after the definition below, run the body of `show_menu`? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: The name followed by round brackets calls the function.
The call on the right runs the body; its result is then stored in `result`.
Without brackets the function is only mentioned, not called, so nothing runs.
This starts a new definition; it doesn't run the existing body.
Python has no `call` keyword. This line is a syntax error.
Calls use round brackets. Empty square brackets after a name aren't valid Python at all: this line is a `SyntaxError`.

explanation: You invoke a function by writing its name followed by round brackets. The call can stand alone or be part of a bigger statement, such as an assignment. Writing the name without brackets doesn't run anything.

code:

print_receipt()

blanks.rationale: A function definition starts with the keyword `def`.
The header needs the brackets and then a colon, which starts the indented body.

stem: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Start`, `Boil water`, `Add tea bag` and `Enjoy`, one per line.
output:
Start
Boil water
Add tea bag
Enjoy
rationale: The body lines must sit directly under the `def` line, the definition must come before the call, and `Enjoy` is printed after the call.
explanation: A `def` prints nothing; it only creates the function. The body is the indented lines under it. The output starts with `Start`, then the call `make_tea()` prints the two body lines, and `Enjoy` comes last. `print("Start")` may also go after the definition, because the definition prints nothing.

stem: Which line, inserted at the marked spot, makes the program print `Morning`, `Rain later` and `Take an umbrella`, one per line?
code:
def check_weather():
    print("Rain later")

print("Morning")
# >>> INSERT <<<
print("Take an umbrella")
output:
Morning
Rain later
Take an umbrella

options.rationale: Without brackets the function is only mentioned, not called, so `Rain later` is never printed.
This starts a new definition with no indented body, so Python reports an `IndentationError`.
The call runs the body, which prints `Rain later` between the other two lines.
This prints the text `check_weather()` instead of calling the function.

explanation: The `def` only creates the function. To run its body you call it: its name followed by round brackets. The call sits between the two `print` lines, so `Rain later` appears between them.

stem: A script reads a file of orders, removes the invalid ones and prints a report. The author writes one function for each of these three steps and calls them in turn. How does this help?

options.text: Python runs the three functions faster than the same steps written as plain lines
options.rationale: Functions don't add speed. The same steps take the same time inside or outside a function.

options.text: Each step has a name and one job, so it is easier to read, test and change on its own
options.rationale: This is decomposition: a big job is split into small named parts that can be understood and fixed separately.

options.text: The functions run on their own, in alphabetical order, so the author need not call them
options.rationale: A function body runs only when it is called. Nothing runs automatically in alphabetical order.

options.text: Any variable created inside one of the functions can be read by the other two
options.rationale: Variables created inside a function are local. The other functions can't see them.

explanation: Splitting a program into functions is called decomposition. Each function does one job and has a name that says what it is, so the main code reads like a list of steps. A bug in the cleaning step can be found and fixed in one small function without touching the rest. Functions don't make code faster, and they only run when they are called.

stem: Which line, inserted at the marked spot, reuses the function so that the program prints a second greeting for Ben?
code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

greet("Ana")
# >>> INSERT <<<

options.rationale: This prints `Hello, Ben`, and then `None`, because `greet` returns nothing and `print()` shows that.
Without brackets this only names the function. It is not a call, so nothing is printed.
Calling the same function with a new argument reuses the code that is already written.
This is not a call. A `def` line needs parameter names, so a string there is a `SyntaxError`.

explanation: Reuse means writing the steps once and calling them many times with different arguments. The call `greet("Ben")` runs the same body with `name` set to `"Ben"`. Leaving out the brackets does not call the function, and a call wrapped in `print()` would also print the returned `None`.

stem: A program contains the definition `def show_menu():`. Which call runs this function?

options.rationale: Python is case-sensitive, so `Show_menu` is a different name and raises a `NameError`.
`show-menu` is read as `show` minus `menu`, which is not the function's name.
The name matches exactly, with the same letters, case and underscore.
The underscore is part of the name. Without it this is another name that was never defined.

explanation: A function name is an identifier: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit and not a keyword. Names are case-sensitive and every character counts, so a call must use exactly the name from the `def` line. A hyphen is never part of a name, because Python reads it as the minus operator.

stem: Which of these are valid names for a function? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Letters and an underscore only, and it is not a keyword.
A name must not start with a digit.
A name may start with an underscore, so this is valid.
A space ends the name. Use an underscore instead.
`class` is a keyword, so it can't be used as a name.

explanation: Valid function names start with a letter or underscore, continue with letters, digits or underscores, and are not keywords. `total_price` and `_helper` follow these rules. `2fast` starts with a digit, `price list` has a space and `class` is reserved by Python.
